topic: The retention consultancy: selling attrition-insurance to small companies with a certified assessment and an AI backend
working_title: Sell Retention to Companies Too Small for Culture Amp
title_options: The 120,000 Dollar Cost of One Person Quitting
Sell Retention to Companies Too Small for Culture Amp
One Person Can Now Run a Retention Practice
thumbnail_concepts: A small-team org chart with one box going dark, and a lost-revenue counter ticking up beside it — the cost of a single departure made visible.
Split screen: a cluttered spreadsheet of raw assessment data on the left, a clean one-page client retention dashboard on the right, the same data transformed.
description_draft: Companies too small for Culture Amp still lose real money every time someone quits — and they have no HR, no analyst, and no platform built for their size. This episode breaks down the business of selling retention to them: a certified assessment as the instrument, an AI backend as the analyst, and you as the judgment and the trust. What a solo operator can realistically make, what the enterprise version proves (Culture Amp, Gallup), the exact sub-$150/month stack, the week-by-week build, and the honest economics — including the three ways it fails. Sourced numbers throughout, hedged where the data is one operator's own. Not an income promise — a documented blueprint with ranges.

beats.vo_text: Welcome in. This is The Operator Economy. A series where we break down one business you can build on your own. This week: selling retention to the companies too small to buy it anywhere else.
beats.asset_hint: slide: series title card

beats.vo_text: One person walking out of a small company can cost it around a hundred and twenty thousand dollars a year. That is one operator's own estimate, from a single practice, but every owner who has lost someone critical feels the shape of it. Companies too small for Culture Amp bleed this quietly, and this is the business that sells them the fix.
highlight_words: a hundred and twenty thousand dollars
beats.asset_hint: chart: what one departure costs a small company, ~$120K/yr flagged as one operator's estimate
beats.source: Operator's own P&L, one practice — stated estimate, unverified

beats.vo_text: This is a consultancy, not a software company. You sell retention as an outcome to companies too small to be worth a seat from the big engagement platforms. Under fifty employees there is usually no HR at all, so the owner is the buyer, and what they are really buying is attrition insurance.
beats.asset_hint: slide: two buyers — owner (5-50) buys the outcome, HR-of-one (50-500) buys capacity

beats.vo_text: The reason one person can run this now is that the analyst layer got cheap. The assessment gives you the instrument, an AI backend does the analysis that used to need a research team, and you provide the judgment and the trust. [POV: the moment you watched one strong person leave a team you ran, and the hole it left that never showed up in any spreadsheet.]
beats.asset_hint: broll: a small team on a floor, one desk quietly emptying out

beats.vo_text: Built small, this is a second income from two or three engagements a year, run around a job. Built seriously, it is a full practice with a renewal engine underneath it. Either way the machine is the same. The first question a skeptic asks is simple. Does anyone actually pay for this?
beats.asset_hint: slide: small build vs serious build — income, renewal engine

beats.vo_text: Start at the low end, and be honest about it. There is no public, verified case study yet of a solo operator running exactly this and posting big numbers. The best evidence at the small end is one practitioner, one certified assessment, and a single pilot engagement delivered so far, unpaid, just to prove the machine runs.
beats.asset_hint: slide: honest gap — no verified solo case study yet, one unpaid pilot to date
beats.source: Operator's ledger — one expedited unpaid pilot; absence of public solo case study stated explicitly

beats.vo_text: The pitch is arithmetic, not adjectives. If one departure costs a small company roughly a hundred and twenty thousand dollars a year, then a five to seven thousand dollar engagement to lower that risk is a rounding error. That first number is one operator's estimate from a single practice, so treat it as directional, but owners recognize the shape of it immediately.
beats.asset_hint: chart: one departure (~$120K/yr) vs a $5–7K engagement, rounding-error framing
beats.source: Operator P&L (stated estimate) + blueprint pricing (estimate, unvalidated)

beats.vo_text: Zoom out one level and the research backs the fear. Replacing an employee runs anywhere from fifty to two hundred percent of their salary, depending on the role and who is counting. Those are analyst estimates with wide ranges, reported not audited, but even the low end of that band is real money to a thirty person company.
beats.asset_hint: chart: cost to replace an employee, 50–200% of salary band, estimate marker visible
beats.source: SHRM / Gallup replacement-cost ranges — analyst estimate, reported

beats.vo_text: Now the high end, to size the market this machine plays in. Gallup puts the global cost of disengaged employees at around eight point eight trillion dollars a year. That is a headline figure, reported, useful for scale and nothing more precise than that. The point is that employers already treat this as real.
beats.asset_hint: chart: Gallup $8.8T global disengagement cost, flagged headline-scale only
beats.source: Gallup State of the Global Workplace — reported headline figure, scale only

beats.vo_text: The clearest proof is the platform the big companies buy. Culture Amp, the enterprise engagement tool, was valued at around one and a half billion dollars back in its 2021 round. That number is dated, and it proves the market, not the moment, but it tells you employers will pay well for exactly the machine you are building at the small end.
highlight_words: one and a half billion dollars
beats.asset_hint: logo: Culture Amp; chart: ~$1.5B valuation (2021), dated marker
beats.source: Press coverage, Culture Amp Series F ~$1.5B valuation (2021), dated

beats.vo_text: So the market is proven at the top and wide open at the bottom, because the platforms priced themselves out of the small company. Culture Amp and Gallup cannot profitably sell a thirty person shop, and the owner still has the problem. That gap is the whole business. So what does the machine that fills it actually cost to build?
beats.asset_hint: slide: proven at the top, open at the bottom — the small-company gap

beats.vo_text: The instrument comes first, and it is the one piece you may not own. A certified assessment gives you the engagement and individual reports the whole method runs on. Verify what your license lets you do with that output before you build anything on top of it, because that contract is the foundation and the biggest risk at once.
beats.asset_hint: slide: the instrument — certified assessment, license terms flagged

beats.vo_text: The analyst is a Claude project, running twenty to a hundred dollars a month depending on volume. You load it with your scoring logic, your spreadsheets, and one anonymized past engagement, and it turns raw assessment data into draft deliverables. It is the piece that used to be a salaried analyst you could not afford.
beats.asset_hint: screen_rec: a Claude project loaded with the methodology, generating a draft dashboard

beats.vo_text: The methodology lives in a spreadsheet, which costs nothing and is what makes the automation possible in the first place. One standardized intake template. Assessment exports, headcount, tenure, turnover history, org structure. If it is not in the template, you do not accept the engagement, because a clean input is what lets the machine run without you rebuilding it every time.
beats.asset_hint: slide: one intake template — exports, headcount, tenure, turnover, org

beats.vo_text: The deliverables are four generated outputs, not four hand builds. A client dashboard as one self-contained web page. A ninety day retention plan. A profile per leader. And the deck that presents it. Each one is a prompt plus a template, and all of it renders for free on top of the tools you already pay for.
beats.asset_hint: slide: four generators — dashboard, 90-day plan, per-leader profiles, deck

beats.vo_text: All in, the fixed cost lands under a hundred and fifty dollars a month, and a portal only enters the picture in phase two, when a paying client asks to log in and track over time. The margin on a five to seven thousand dollar engagement, priced as an estimate for now, is basically your time. So how do you turn this stack into a first paying client?
highlight_words: under a hundred and fifty dollars
beats.asset_hint: chart: monthly stack cost, under $150 total
beats.source: public pricing — stack totals (< $150/mo); engagement price is blueprint estimate

beats.vo_text: Week one is not sales, it is foundations. Confirm in writing what your assessment license permits, and if the terms are restrictive, swap in an instrument you own, because the machine does not care which assessment feeds it. Then build the single intake template that every future engagement will run through.
beats.asset_hint: slide: Week 1 — verify license, standardize intake

beats.vo_text: Week two, build the four generators and run your one pilot's real data through them, start to finish. What comes out the other side is not a practice exercise. It is your sales demo, built from a real engagement, and it is the thing you show instead of describing what you would theoretically do.
beats.asset_hint: screen_rec: pilot data running through the four generators into a finished dashboard

beats.vo_text: Month one, you sell the first segment, the owner with no HR, and you start inside your own network. The opener is that hundred and twenty thousand dollar line, which is one operator's estimate, and the proof is a turnaround measured in days, not the weeks a big platform would take. [POV: how you would actually open that first conversation with an owner you already know, in your own words, without it sounding like a pitch.]
beats.asset_hint: slide: Month 1 — sell the owner segment from warm network, $120K opener

beats.vo_text: Price the first engagement as a founding client, discounted on purpose, in exchange for a named case study and permission to use the before and after numbers. You are not buying revenue yet. You are buying the one trend line you could not inherit, because no public case study for this exists at the small end.
beats.asset_hint: slide: founding engagement — discount for a named case study + trend data

beats.vo_text: Months two and three, run the ninety day loop. Two weeks to baseline and deliver the dashboard and plan. Then the human weeks, the leadership work and the hard conversations that AI does not touch. Then re-measure, show the updated numbers, and have the renewal conversation. With one trend line in hand, you can finally pitch the HR of one at a bigger company. So what does this actually pay?
beats.asset_hint: slide: 90-day loop — baseline, human weeks, re-measure, renew

beats.vo_text: We turned this whole build, the intake template, the four generators, and the pricing logic, into a blueprint you can download free, linked below, if you would rather start from a checklist than a transcript.
beats.asset_hint: slide: blueprint cover — The Retention Consultancy, step by step

beats.vo_text: The honest range for year one is fifteen to thirty thousand dollars, from two or three engagements at five to seven thousand each. That is an estimate reasoned from one unpaid pilot and the pricing logic, not audited revenue, and it assumes your warm network produces the first client.
beats.asset_hint: chart: realistic year-one range, $15–30K from 2–3 engagements, estimate marker
beats.source: Blueprint economics — estimate, reasoned from one pilot, unvalidated

beats.vo_text: The first failure mode is the license. If you build your whole delivery machine on an assessment you do not own, that is platform risk in a lab coat. One change to the vendor's terms and your practice stops. Verify it in week one, or own the instrument outright.
beats.asset_hint: slide: failure mode 1 — license / platform risk

beats.vo_text: The second failure mode is selling up-market. Above five hundred employees the money looks bigger, and the procurement cycles, security reviews, and incumbents will bury a solo operator. [POV: your own read on why owners of small companies drag their feet on turnover until someone critical actually quits.]
beats.asset_hint: slide: failure mode 2 — the 500+ trap (procurement, incumbents)

beats.vo_text: The third is distribution, and it is the quiet one. AI compresses delivery from weeks to days, and does nothing for your pipeline. Your first clients come from people who already trust you, and that part stays manual. Which leaves one real open question. Does a ninety day engagement renew into a standing retainer, or stay a one time project?
beats.asset_hint: slide: failure mode 3 — distribution; open question: does it renew?

blueprint_summary.idea: Sell retention as an outcome to companies too small for the enterprise engagement platforms: a certified assessment as the instrument, an AI backend as the analyst that turns raw assessment data into a dashboard, a 90-day plan, per-leader profiles and a deck, and you as the judgment and the trust.
blueprint_summary.who_its_for: Operators who've managed teams or owned a practice — ex-owners, ex-HR leads, ex-ops managers, clinicians who ran a floor — who want a consulting practice with a renewal engine, not a software company.
evidence_companies: The solo practitioner (this blueprint's subject, anonymized — one certified assessment, one unpaid pilot)

tool_stack.role: The analyst: intake → analysis → 90-day plan → per-leader profiles → deck
The instrument: engagement + individual reports the method runs on
tool_stack.monthly_cost: Contracted — verify license terms before building on the output

tool_stack.role: Methodology home + one standardized intake template
Client deliverable — one self-contained page per client, generated not hand-built
Client login + tracking over time + email cadence, built when a client asks to log in

blueprint_summary.first_customer_plan: Week 1: verify the assessment license and build one intake template. Week 2: build the four generators and dry-run your pilot's real data into a finished demo. Month 1: sell the owner-with-no-HR segment from your warm network, opening with the ~$120K departure cost and a days-not-weeks turnaround; price the first as a discounted founding client for a named case study and the trend data. Months 2–3: run the 90-day loop (baseline → human leadership weeks → re-measure → renewal), then use the trend line to open the HR-of-one segment at 50–500-person companies.
blueprint_summary.realistic_economics: Year-one realistic range $15–30K from 2–3 engagements at $5–7.5K — a strong second income, not a startup, and an estimate reasoned from one unpaid pilot. Fixed cost under $150/mo. Three failure modes: (1) license/platform risk if you build on an assessment you don't own; (2) selling up-market above 500 employees where procurement and incumbents bury a solo operator; (3) distribution — AI compresses delivery, not pipeline, so first clients still come from existing trust. Open question the pilot will answer: does the 90-day engagement renew into a standing retainer.
